paragraph: Kenya's population is estimated at approximately 57.5 million in 2025, making it one of the most populous countries in East Africa. In 1960, the country had roughly 8.1 million people, increasing to 16.6 million by 1980. By 2000, the population had reached approximately 30.7 million, before rising to around 53.0 million in 2020. This growth reflects high birth rates, improvements in healthcare, and declining mortality over several decades.

Tanzania has experienced substantial population growth, reaching approximately 70.5 million people in 2025. Its population was around 10.0 million in 1960 and increased to approximately 18.5 million by 1980. By 2000, Tanzania had roughly 34.0 million inhabitants, compared with approximately 61.7 million in 2020. Expanding access to healthcare and persistently high fertility rates have contributed to this long-term increase.

Ghana's population is estimated at approximately 35.1 million in 2025. Historical figures show that the country had around 6.6 million inhabitants in 1960, increasing to approximately 11.9 million in 1980. By 2000, the population had grown to roughly 19.5 million, reaching approximately 32.8 million by 2020. Urbanization and improvements in public health have accompanied this demographic expansion.

Morocco has an estimated population of approximately 38.4 million in 2025. In 1960, its population was around 12.3 million, rising to approximately 20.4 million by 1980. The population reached roughly 28.8 million in 2000 and approximately 36.7 million in 2020. Declining mortality and improvements in life expectancy have played important roles in the country's demographic development.

Saudi Arabia's population is estimated at approximately 34.6 million in 2025. In 1960, the country had roughly 4.1 million inhabitants, increasing to approximately 9.6 million by 1980. Its population reached around 21.1 million in 2000 and approximately 32.8 million in 2020. Economic development, immigration, and relatively high fertility rates have all contributed to population growth.

South Korea has an estimated population of approximately 51.7 million in 2025. Its population was around 25.0 million in 1960 and increased to approximately 38.1 million by 1980. By 2000, the population had reached roughly 46.8 million, before growing to approximately 51.8 million in 2020. Unlike many developing countries, South Korea now faces demographic challenges associated with extremely low fertility and an aging population.

Malaysia's population is estimated at approximately 36.0 million in 2025. In 1960, the country had around 8.2 million people, increasing to approximately 13.8 million by 1980. Its population reached roughly 23.2 million in 2000 and approximately 33.4 million in 2020. Economic development, urbanization, and natural population growth have contributed to these demographic changes.

Poland's population is estimated at approximately 38.1 million in 2025. In 1960, the country had roughly 29.6 million inhabitants, increasing to approximately 35.6 million by 1980. Its population reached around 38.3 million in 2000 and approximately 38.0 million in 2020. More recently, low fertility rates, emigration, and an aging population have contributed to demographic stagnation and decline.

The Netherlands has an estimated population of approximately 18.3 million in 2025. Its population was around 11.5 million in 1960, increasing to approximately 14.1 million by 1980. By 2000, the population had reached roughly 15.9 million, rising to approximately 17.4 million in 2020. Immigration, natural population growth, and increasing life expectancy have contributed to this steady expansion.

Sweden's population is estimated at approximately 10.7 million in 2025. In 1960, the country had around 7.5 million inhabitants, increasing to approximately 8.3 million by 1980. Its population reached roughly 8.9 million in 2000 and approximately 10.4 million in 2020. Immigration, relatively high life expectancy, and gradual population growth have helped shape Sweden's demographic trends.
